title: Third Explosive Drone Found Near Leipzig Airport as Europe Confronts Russian Hybrid Warfare
excerpt: U.S. intelligence links the attack to Russian military intelligence after an armed drone was discovered near a Ukrainian cargo plane carrying ammunition at a key NATO logistics hub.
body:
• German investigators found a third explosive drone and 50 grams of military-grade hexogen near Leipzig/Halle airport, 10 days after the initial attack on August 4
  • U.S. intelligence has linked the explosive drone to Russian military intelligence; the device was found near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane carrying military ammunition
  • A second drone collided with a DHL cargo plane that aborted its landing, causing minor damage; investigators believe the detonator on the first drone malfunctioned
  • The incident represents what Germany calls a "new level of danger" as Europe confronts escalating hybrid warfare targeting aviation and logistics infrastructure

German investigators have discovered a third drone and suspected military explosives linked to this month's attempted attack on Leipzig/Halle airport, according to reports by NDR, WDR, and the Süddeutsche Zeitung, deepening concerns about a sustained campaign of sabotage targeting European aviation infrastructure.

The third drone was found on August 14, ten days after the initial incident, to the west of the airport. Investigators also recovered approximately 50 grams of a substance they believe to be hexogen, a military-grade explosive, the reports said.

A Failed Attack on Military Supply Lines

The crisis began on the night of August 4, when an airport employee spotted a quadcopter drone on the tarmac in a restricted area near Ukrainian Antonov cargo planes at the Leipzig/Halle facility — one of NATO's key logistics hubs in eastern Germany and an operating base for Ukraine's Antonov Airlines since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.

The drone was equipped with explosives and a detonator, according to prosecutors. German newspaper Bild reported that investigators believe only a technical malfunction prevented the device from detonating. The Ukrainian cargo plane nearest to the drone was carrying military ammunition, the Times reported, heightening suspicions that the attack was aimed at disrupting weapons deliveries to Ukraine.

"Such threat situations are not carried out by amateurs, but must be prepared very professionally and executed professionally."

— Alexander Dobrindt, German Interior Minister

A second unidentified flying object — which investigators suspect was a surveillance drone possibly carrying a camera to record the attack — collided with a DHL cargo plane that had aborted its landing at Leipzig due to the airport closure. The jet sustained minor damage and diverted to Hanover.

U.S. Intelligence Points to Russia

The explosive-laden drone likely belongs to the Russian government, according to U.S. officials familiar with intelligence reports about the incident, the Wall Street Journal reported. German federal prosecutors launched a probe describing the event as "a serious attack on the transportation and logistics infrastructure in Germany" that posed a threat to the country's external and internal security.

Russia's embassy in Berlin dismissed the incident as a "fabricated provocation," saying it was another example of accusations without evidence. "It is obvious that this hastily fabricated provocation only serves the interests of Kyiv and the militarist wing of the European political class," the embassy said in a statement.

A Continent on Alert

The Leipzig incident is the latest in a pattern of suspected Russian hybrid operations across Europe. Drones have disrupted flights at airports across the continent, NATO airspace has been violated in Poland and Romania, and underwater cables have been severed in the Baltic Sea. In 2024, incendiary devices were found concealed in parcels at a DHL warehouse in Leipzig and in freight shipments across Europe, though investigators have not confirmed a direct connection to the August 4 attack.

France's top general has separately warned that the country is "not ready to face cheap drones yet," underscoring the broader vulnerability across European defense establishments.

"We have known about suspicious drone flights over Germany for years. However, a drone equipped with an explosive device and detonator represents a new level of severity."

— Peter Neumann, Professor of Security Studies, King's College London

What Comes Next

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned that attackers would "pay the price," though he stopped short of naming Russia directly. The incident has intensified debate within NATO about the blurring line between peacetime and conflict. The incoming head of Britain's MI6 warned in December that the UK is "now operating in a space between peace and war" with "the front line everywhere."

Security agencies across Europe are now reassessing the vulnerability of airports, military bases, and logistics infrastructure to low-cost drone attacks — a threat that has moved from the battlefields of Ukraine into the heart of the continent.
